'''Joel Lee Brenner''' ({{birth date|1912|8|2}} – {{death date|1997|11|14}}) was an American [[mathematician]] who specialized in [[matrix theory]], [[linear algebra]], and [[group theory]]. He is known as the translator of several popular [[Russian language|Russian]] texts. He was a teaching professor at some dozen colleges and universities and was a Senior Mathematician at [[Stanford Research Institute]] from 1956 to 1968. He published over one hundred scholarly papers, 35 with coauthors, and wrote book reviews.<ref name= ams>{{cite journal|year=1998|title=Mathematics People|journal=Notices of the AMS|volume=45|issue=4|publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]|url=https://www.ams.org/notices/199804/people.pdf|access-date=18 December 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url= http://orlabs.oclc.org/identities/lccn-n88-678822|title= Brenner, J. L. (Joel Lee) |author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |access-date=1 January 2013}}</ref><ref name=Beasley>LeRoy B. Beasley (1987) "The Mathematical Work of Joel Lee Brenner", [[Linear Algebra and its Applications]] 90:1–13</ref>

==Academic career==
In 1930 Brenner earned a B.A. degree with major in [[chemistry]] from [[Harvard University]]. In graduate study there he was influenced by Hans Brinkmann, [[Garrett Birkhoff]], and [[Marshall Stone]]. He was granted the Ph.D. in February 1936.<ref name=Beasley/> Brenner later described some of his [[reminiscence]]s of his student days at Harvard and of the state of American mathematics in the 1930s in an article for [[American Mathematical Monthly]].<ref>Brenner (1979) "Student Days", [[American Mathematical Monthly]] 86: 359–6</ref>

In 1951 Brenner published his findings about matrices with [[quaternion]] entries.<ref>{{cite journal
|author = J. L. Brenner
|title = Matrices of quaternions
|journal = Pacific Journal of Mathematics
|volume = 1
|year = 1951
|pages =  329–335
|issue = 1951
|doi=10.2140/pjm.1951.1.329|doi-access = free
}}</ref> He developed the idea of a [[characteristic root]] of a quaternion matrix (an eigenvalue) and shows that they must exist. He also shows that a quaternion matrix is unitarily-equivalent to a [[triangular matrix]].

In 1956 he became a Senior Mathematician at [[Stanford Research Institute]].
Brenner, in collaboration with Donald W. Bushaw and S. Evanusa, assisted in the translation and revision of [[Felix Gantmacher]]'s ''Applications of the Theory of Matrices'' (1959).<ref>George Weiss (1960) Review ''Applications of the Theory of Matrices'', [[Science (journal)|Science]] 131: 405,6, issue #3398</ref>

Brenner translated [[Nikolay Krasovsky|Nikolaj Nikolaevič Krasovskii's]] book ''Stability of motion: applications of Lyapunov's second method to differential systems and equations with delay'' (1963). He also translated and edited the book ''Problems in differential equations'' by [[Aleksei Fedorovich Filippov]].

Brenner translated ''Problems in Higher Algebra''<ref>Сборник задач по высшей алгебре</ref> by [[D. K. Faddeev]] and I.S. Sominiski. The [[exercise (mathematics)|exercise]]s in this book covered [[complex number]]s, [[roots of unity]], as well as some [[linear algebra]] and [[abstract algebra]].

In 1959 Brenner generalized propositions by [[Alexander Ostrowski]] and [[G. B. Price]] on [[minor (linear algebra)|minor]]s of a [[diagonally dominant matrix]].<ref>{{cite journal|author = J. L. Brenner|title = Relations among the minors of a matrix with dominant principal diagonal|journal = [[Duke Mathematical Journal]]|volume = 26|year = 1959| issue=4 |pages =  563–567|doi = 10.1215/S0012-7094-59-02653-5}}</ref> His work is credited with stimulating a reawakening of interest in the [[permanent (mathematics)|permanent]] of a matrix.<ref>Henryk Minc (1978) ''Permanents'', page 13, Encyclopedia of Mathematics and its Applications volume 6, [[Addison-Wesley]]</ref>

One of the challenges in linear algebra is to find the [[eigenvalues and eigenvectors]] of a square matrix of complex numbers. In 1931 [[S. A. Gershgorin]] described geometric bounds on the eigenvectors in terms of the matrix elements. This result known as the [[Gershgorin circle theorem]] has been used as a basis for extension. In 1964 Brenner reported on ''Theorems of Gersgorin Type''.<ref>Brenner (January 1964) [https://apps.dtic.mil/sti/citations/AD0433879 Theorems of Gersgorin type], citation from [[Defense Technical Information Center]].</ref> In 1967 at [[University of Wisconsin—Madison]], working in the Mathematics Research Center, he produced a technical report ''New root-location theorems for partitioned matrices''.<ref>J. L. Brenner (1967) [https://apps.dtic.mil/sti/citations/AD0662744 New root-location theorems for partitioned matrices], citation from Defense Technical Information Center</ref>

In 1968 Brenner, following [[Alston Householder]], published "Gersgorin theorems by Householder’s proof".<ref>Brenner (1968) [https://projecteuclid.org/euclid.bams/1183529651 Gersgorin theorems by Householder’s proof], [[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society]] 74:3, link from [[Project Euclid]]</ref> In 1970 he published the survey article (21 references) "Gersgorin theorems, regularity theorems, and bounds for determinants of partitioned matrices".<ref>Brenner (1970) "Gersgorin theorems, regularity theorems, and bounds for determinants of partitioned matrices", SIAM Journal for Applied Mathematics 19(2)</ref> The article was extended with "Some determinantal identities".<ref>Brenner (1971) ) [http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.pjm/1102969768 Gersgorin theorems, regularity theorems, and bounds for determinants of partitioned matrices, and some determinantal identities], [[Pacific Journal of Mathematics]] 39(1), link from Project Euclid</ref>

In 1971 Brenner extended his geometry of the spectrum of a square complex matrix deeper into abstract algebra with his paper "Regularity theorems and Gersgorin theorems for matrices over rings with valuation".<ref>Brenner (1971) [http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.rmjm/1250131822 Regularity theorems and Gersgorin theorems for matrices over rings with valuation], [[Rocky Mountain Journal of Mathematics]] 1(3), link from Project Euclid</ref> He writes, "Theorems can be extended to non-commutative domains, in particular to [[quaternion]] matrices. Secondly, the [[ring of polynomials]] has a valuation ... a different type of regularity ..."

==Collaborations==

Joel Lee Brenner was a member of the [[American Mathematical Society]] from 1936.

Beasley relates that he
:was a graduate student and [Brenner] was visiting the [[University of British Columbia]] in 1966-67. Shortly after arriving at UBC, Joel circulated a memo to all the graduate students, informing them that he had several open problems in various areas of mathematics and would share them with willing students. Hoping to get a problem in [[group theory]] that I might work into a thesis, I went to his office and inquired about the problems. He presented me the Van der Waerden conjecture, which he informed me would be quite difficult, and after defining the [[permanent (mathematics)|permanent]] for me sent me off with several problems concerning the permanent function. His encouragement and enthusiasm persevered through several "proofs" of the [[permanent (mathematics)#Van der Waerden's conjecture|Van der Waerden conjecture]], and soon some of the less well-known problems had been solved. He would always tell me how a proposed attack would work and leave me to fight out the details. Those exchanges led to the publication of my first paper, and I became his thirteenth coauthor. By the time Joel had left UBC in the spring of 1967, I was firmly entrenched in matrix theory.<ref name=Beasley/>{{rp|3}}

In 1981 Brenner and [[Roger Lyndon]] collaborated to polish an idea due to [[H. W. Kuhn]] for proving the [[fundamental theorem of algebra]]. In the solution by Eric S. Rosenthal to a problem in the ''American Mathematical Monthly'' posted by Harry D. Ruderman,<ref>Solution to problem #6192, ''American Mathematical Monthly'' 86: 598</ref> Kuhn's work from 1974 was cited. A query was made and prompted an article by Brenner and Lyndon.<ref>J. L. Brenner & [[R. C. Lyndon]] (1981) "Proof of the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra", ''American Mathematical Monthly'' 88(4):254–6</ref> The version of the fundamental theorem stated was as follows:
:Let ''P''(''z'') be a non-constant polynomial with complex coefficients. Then there is a positive number ''S'' > 0, depending only on ''P'', with the following property:
:: for every δ > 0 there is a complex number ''z'' such that |''z''| ≤ ''S'' and |''P''(''z'')| < δ .

Brenner ultimately acquired 35 coauthors in his publications.

===Alternating group===
Given an ordered set Ω with ''n'' elements, the [[even permutation]]s on it determine the [[alternating group]] A<sub>n</sub>. In 1960 Brenner proposed the following research problem in group theory:<ref>Brenner (1960) [https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/1960-66-04/S0002-9904-1960-10468-5/S0002-9904-1960-10468-5.pdf Research Problem in Group Theory], [[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society]] 66(4):275</ref> For which A<sub>n</sub> does there exist an element ''a''<sub>n</sub> such that every element ''g'' is similar to a [[commutator]] of ''a''<sub>n</sub>? Brenner states that the property is true for 4 < ''n'' < 10; in symbols it may be expressed
:<math>\exists a_n \ \forall g \ \exists u \ \exists y \ (g = u^{-1}(a_n y a_n^{-1} y^{-1}) u) .</math>
The alternating groups are [[simple group]]s, and in 1971 Brenner began a series of articles titled "Covering theorems for finite simple groups". He was interested in the [[cycle type]] of [[cyclic permutation]]s, and when A<sub>n</sub> ⊂ ''C C'', where ''C'' is a [[conjugacy class]] of a certain type.<ref>Brenner, R.M. Cranwell, and J. Riddell (1975) [https://msp.org/pjm/1975/58-1/p05.xhtml Covering theorems: V],  [[Pacific Journal of Mathematics]] 58: 55–60</ref><ref>Brenner & L. Carlitz (1976) [[Rendiconti del Seminario Matematico della Università di Padova]] 55:81–90</ref><ref>Brenner (1978) "Covering theorems for FINASIGS", [[Journal of the Australian Mathematical Society]] 25A: 210–14</ref>

In 1977 he posed the question, "What permutations in A<sub>n</sub> can be expressed as a product of permutations of periods k and l" ?<ref>Brenner & J. Riddell (1977) ''American Mathematical Monthly'' 84(1): 39–40</ref>

==Works==

In 1987 [[Linear Algebra and its Applications]] published a list of 111 articles by J.L. Brenner, and the four books he translated.<ref name=Beasley/>
